extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of political science, constitutional law, and legislative procedure
extracted.subtask_description: Summaries and normative observations about lobbying practice, committee procedure, and specific constitutional provisions (Confederate Constitution, Canadian Federal Constitution, Dartmouth case, Articles of Confederation). Contains suggested legal standards, statutory references, and historical commentary on acceptable/illegitimate behavior in legislative settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee referral and deference
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress refers all public bills as well as private bills to committees; legislatures have formed the habit of accepting generally, though not invariably, the decisions of a committee upon the bills it has dealt with.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the multitude of bills and difficulty of discussing them in a large body, committees investigate and their reports are often decisive; this concentrates advocacy efforts on committees and creates incentives to influence committee members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee discretion in evidence and amendment
rubrics_metrics.description: The committees ... inquire into and amend bills in their uncontrolled discretion, upon such evidence or other statements as they choose to admit or use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees lack strict quasi-judicial rules in America and thus may admit or exclude evidence at will; advocates should be aware that committee procedure (as opposed to formal court procedure) governs how arguments and evidence are received.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimate methods of lobbying
rubrics_metrics.description: A measure ... may be urged upon members of the legislative body in every form of influence except the pecuniary one. By casual interviews, by informal conversation, by formal presentation of facts and arguments, by printed appeals in pamphlet form, by newspaper communications and leading articles, by personal introductions ... by dinners, receptions, and other entertainments ... the public man is beset to look favourably upon the measure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mr. Spofford's formulation: lobbying is frequently legitimate when it consists of presentation and proof of facts, testimony, arguments, printed or personal appeals to reason and justice; these forms of influence are acceptable and necessary to bring facts fairly before the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on pecuniary influence (statutory)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutes have been passed severely punishing any person who offers any money or value to any member with a view to influence his vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As to Congress, see §5450 of the Revised Statutes of the United States; many States have analogous provisions. Offering money/value to influence votes is criminalized and a primary legal limit on lobbying.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contracts to influence legislation (void if secret/other-than-open)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracts which have for their object to influence legislation in any other manner than by such open and public presentation of facts, arguments, and appeals to reason, such as are recognized as proper and legitimate with all public bodies, must be held void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have repeatedly held secret or covert contractual arrangements to influence legislation invalid; Frost v. Belmont and commentary in Cooley support refusal to enforce such contracts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quasi-judicial standard for private-bill committees (England)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each member of a private bill committee is to be considered as a quasi-judicial person, whose vote neither a brother member nor any outsider may attempt to influence, but who is bound to decide, as far as he can, in a judicial spirit on the footing of the evidence tendered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: England adopted a semi-judicial procedure for private bills and created parliamentary agents bound by professional rules; this institutional design was a response to lobbying abuses during intense railway-era private-bill litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of secret consultations and 'lobby members'
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of 'lobby members' is not to go fairly and openly before the committees and present statements, proofs, and arguments, that the other side has an opportunity to meet and refute ... but to go secretly to the members and ply them with statements and arguments that the other side cannot openly meet ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secret consultations, log-rolling, and inducements via entertainment or food are condemned as tending to render members unfit to decide; courts and commentators decry practices that prevent open presentation and rebuttal of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal for authorized agents before committees
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been suggested that a regular body of attorneys, authorized to act as agents before committees of Congress, should be created.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A bill for this purpose was laid before the Senate in 1875; the suggestion aims to professionalize and regulate representation before committees (analogous to parliamentary agents in England).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lobbyist disclosure and reporting requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Massachusetts endeavoured by Statute to regulate her State lobby, by requiring every person promoting a bill to state whom he has employed for the purpose and what he has paid. New York, Missouri, and other States have also passed laws designed to regulate and check lobbying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure statutes have had some beneficial effect but the evils of lobbying have not been completely extirpated; reporting/employment disclosure is one regulatory tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee composition risks (inexperience)
rubrics_metrics.description: The committees ... are largely composed of new men, unused to the exercise of the powers entrusted to them, though in the House of Representatives the chairman is a person of some experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inexperience among committee members increases the value of skilled lobbyists' influence and can lead to less predictable or more manipulable committee outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Difference in treatment of private bills (England vs America)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas in England private bills are dealt with by a semi-judicial procedure, the promoters and opponents appearing by professional agents and barristers, in America no such procedure has been created, either in Congress or in the State legislatures, and private bills are handled much like public ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional difference explains stronger professional safeguards in England and more informal, lobby-prone processes in the United States.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impeachment by state legislature (Confederate Constitution Art. I §2)
rubrics_metrics.description: A provision is inserted permitting the impeachment of a Federal officer acting within the limits of any State by a vote of two-thirds of the legislature thereof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the Confederate Constitution's variations from the Federal Constitution intended to increase state control over federal officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Departmental officer access to legislative floor (Confederate Art. I §6)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress may by law grant to the principal officer in each of the executive departments, a seat upon the floor of either House, with the privilege of discussing any measure appertaining to his department.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A slight approximation towards a Cabinet system, allowing executive officers direct speaking access in the legislature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Item veto for appropriations (Confederate Art. I §7)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is permitted to veto any particular item or items in an appropriation bill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Considered by the author as an obvious improvement in some respects—gives the executive more precise control over spending.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibitions on protective duties and bounties (Confederate Art. I §8)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imposition of protective duties and the granting of bounties on industry are forbidden, and the granting of money for internal improvements is strictly limited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confederate provisions restrict federal economic intervention; the author regards some of these changes as improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strict appropriation rules (Confederate Art. I §9)
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress is forbidden to appropriate money from the Treasury, except by a vote of two-thirds of both Houses, unless it be asked by the head of a department and submitted by the President, or be for the payment of its own expenses, or of claims against the Confederacy, declared by a judicial tribunal to be just.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limits ordinary legislative control over appropriations, increasing executive/departmental or judicial checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential term and eligibility (Confederate Art. II §1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President and Vice-President are to be elected for six years, and the President is not to be re-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer fixed term with single non-repeatable tenure—an important structural difference from the U.S. Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential removal powers (Confederate Art. II §2)
rubrics_metrics.description: The President is given power to remove the highest officials at his pleasure, and others for good cause, reporting the removals to the Senate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expands executive control over appointments and removals, subject to reporting duties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amending process by convention (Confederate Art. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: The process for amending the Constitution is to be by a Convention of all the States, followed by the ratification of two-thirds of the States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A different constitutional amendment route emphasizing state conventions and supermajority ratification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cabinet (ministerial) responsibility in Dominion (Canadian Federal Constitution)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal or Dominion Government is conducted on the so-called 'Cabinet system' of England, i.e. the Ministry sit in Parliament, and hold office at the pleasure of the House of Commons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canada adopted responsible government: ministers are accountable to Parliament, unlike a strict presidential separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governor-General, Senate, and judiciary composition and powers (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Governor-General is in the position of an irresponsible and permanent executive similar to that of the Crown ... He can dissolve Parliament. The Upper House or Senate is composed of 87 persons, nominated for life by the Governor-General ... The judges ... are appointed by the Crown ... and hold for good behaviour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes appointment methods and distribution of formal powers—Governor-General's reserve powers and Senate composition limit its power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provincial legislature structure and Lieutenant-Governor veto (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each of the Provinces ... has a legislature of its own, which ... in some consists of one House only, and a Lieutenant-Governor, appointed by the Dominion Government, with a right of veto on the acts of the legislature, which he seldom exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provincial systems vary; Lieutenant-Governor is a Crown representative with rarely used veto power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of legislative powers (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whereas in the United States, Congress has only the powers actually granted to it, the Dominion Parliament has a general power of legislation, restricted only by the grant of certain specific and exclusive powers to the Provincial legislatures (§§ 91–95). Criminal law is reserved for the Dominion Parliament; and no province has the right to maintain a military force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The allocation gives the Dominion broad residual authority and central control over criminal law and defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional amendment and origin (Canada)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution of the Dominion was never submitted to popular vote, and can be altered only by the British Parliament, except as regards certain points left to its own legislature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The BNA Act (1867) was enacted by the British Parliament; popular amendment mechanisms are limited compared with, e.g., U.S. state constitutional amendment by popular vote.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contract clause protection for corporate charters (Dartmouth College case)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court ... held that the original charter constituted a contract between the crown ... and the trustees of the college, which was impaired by the act of the legislature ... The act of a government ... which creates a corporation, is a contract between the state and the corporation, and ... becomes, when accepted by it, contracts within the meaning of the [Constitution's contract clause].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dartmouth College v. Woodward (1818) established that charters are contracts protected from state impairment; the doctrine has been somewhat qualified since, requiring existence of an actual contract when relief is sought.

rubrics_metrics.name: State reserve power to vary grants/contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: It has also become the practice for States making contracts by grants to which the principle of this decision could apply, to reserve power to vary or annul them, so as to leave the hands of the State free.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States may include reservation clauses to preserve legislative flexibility despite contract-clause concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: States retain sovereignty except delegated powers (Articles of Confederation Art. II)
rubrics_metrics.description: Each State retains its sovereignty, freedom, and independence, and every power, jurisdiction, and right, which is not by this confederation expressly delegated to the United States in Congress assembled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under the Articles of Confederation the states were sovereign except as to expressly delegated matters; a fundamental feature of the confederation model.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privileges, immunities, and free ingress among states (Articles Art. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: The free inhabitants of each of these States ... shall be entitled to all privileges and immunities of free citizens in the several States; and the people of each State shall have free ingress and regress to and from any other State, and shall enjoy therein all the privileges of trade and commerce ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Promotes free movement and common commercial privileges among states, subject to limited exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extradition of fugitives (Articles Art. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: If any person guilty of, or charged with, treason, felony, or other high misdemeanour in any State, shall flee from justice, and be found in any of the United States, he shall, upon demand of the governor ... be delivered up, and removed to the State having jurisdiction of his offence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides interstate extradition mechanisms for serious crimes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full faith and credit among states (Articles Art. IV)
rubrics_metrics.description: Full faith and credit shall be given, in each of these States, to the records, acts, and judicial proceedings of the courts and magistrates of every other State.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires recognition of other states' legal acts and records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegate appointment, tenure, and incompatibility rules (Articles Art. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Delegates shall be annually appointed ... No State shall be represented in Congress by less than two, nor by more than seven members: and no person shall be capable of being a delegate for more than three years, in any term of six years; nor shall any person, being a delegate, be capable of holding any office under the United States ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies representative selection, limits on continuous service, and incompatibility with other federal offices.

rubrics_metrics.name: State equality in Congress and voting (Articles Art. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining questions in the United States, in Congress assembled, each State shall have one vote.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confederal equality: each state, regardless of size, had a single vote in Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom of speech and protection from arrest for members (Articles Art. V)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freedom of speech and debate in Congress shall not be impeached or questioned in any court or place out of Congress; and the members of Congress shall be protected in their persons from arrests ... during the time of their going to and from, and attendance in Congress, except for treason, felony, or breach of the peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immunities for legislative deliberation and limited arrest protections intended to secure independent legislative functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on states' foreign relations and titles (Articles Art. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: No State, without the consent of the United States, in Congress assembled, shall send any embassy to, or receive any embassy from ... nor shall any person holding any office of profit or trust under the United States ... accept of any present, emolument, office, or title ... from any king, prince, or foreign state; nor shall the United States ... grant any title of nobility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralizes foreign relations and forbids acceptance of foreign titles/emoluments by federal officers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on state military/naval forces and war (Articles Art. VI)
rubrics_metrics.description: No vessels of war shall be kept up in time of peace by any State, except such number only as shall be deemed necessary by the United States ... nor shall any body of forces be kept up by any State ... but every State shall always keep up a well-regulated and disciplined militia ... No State shall engage in any war without the consent of the United States ... unless such State be actually invaded ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Places limits on state military/naval autonomy, preserves federal control over war-making and defense except in immediate self-defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appointment of officers for land forces (Articles Art. VII)
rubrics_metrics.description: When land forces are raised by any State for the common defence, all officers of or under the rank of colonel shall be appointed by the legislature of each State respectively by whom such forces shall be raised ... and all vacancies shall be filled up by the State which first made the appointment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifies state-level control over most officer appointments for troops raised for the common defence under the Articles.
